53c36daa-840c-48b3-b071-b5070021e016.one_liner: A granular look at how private credit and leveraged finance are now pricing GPU/NeoCloud collateral risk, plus a skeptic's breakdown of why AI capex revenue math doesn't close -- a genuinely new structured-credit asset class forming in real time.
53c36daa-840c-48b3-b071-b5070021e016.recap: Odd Lots runs two linked segments. First, Stanley Lee of Liquid Compute (ex-Barclays HY/CDS, ex-Point72) explains how GPU compute has become a credit and financing ecosystem, not just a marketplace. Mid-market NeoCloud operators borrow against GPU clusters via multi-year amortizing loans, with off-taker creditworthiness (large AI labs) originally the main underwriting factor; now operator execution risk matters more too. LTVs have fallen from ~80% over the summer to 70% post-Labor Day to 50-60% now, forcing NeoClouds to demand higher customer prepayments or raise their own holdco equity. Lee argues GPU rental-rate indices (B200/B300) are rising partly from genuine demand but increasingly from buyers' cost-of-capital constraints, since VCs fund much of the 'demand' rather than revenue. He draws analogies to post-2008 aircraft finance (prepayments, re-let markets, appraisals) and flags growing private-credit demand for put-option hedges on rental indices -- a nascent CDS-like product -- plus the critical, often unverified, assumption that defaulted capacity can be quickly 're-let' (transferring SSH keys) rather than physically repossessed. Second, Paul Kedrosky (SK Ventures/Oxford) argues that the project-finance math behind AI capex doesn't close: hitting reasonable hurdle rates by ~2032 requires $3-6 trillion in annual AI revenue, achievable only via deep enterprise substitution, which so far shows up only in coding. He cites exploding software vulnerability counts (50% of all-time critical CVEs found in H1 2026) benefiting reinsurers' pricing power, not productivity.

6a4809cb-d7a5-49eb-8242-b50701559401.recap: Bloomberg's Credit Edge hosts James Crumby and David Havens interview Kevin Magid, CEO of Audax Private Debt, on the state of private credit. Magid pushes back on "golden age is over" headlines, arguing underwriting quality, not market-level panic, determines outcomes. He distinguishes Audax's core middle-market segment (EBITDA $15-75mm, loans sized ~$100-175mm at ~5x leverage) from large-cap private credit and broadly syndicated loans, where AI-driven "SaaS apocalypse" stress has hit software loans trading in the 80s and some restructurings. Audax has made zero ARR (annual recurring revenue) loans, lending only against trailing 12-month EBITDA rather than projected growth, which he credits for avoiding losses. He cites 26-year loss rates of 6bp on senior secured and 17bp on junior/mezzanine debt, versus current market non-accrual rates near 2% and default rates of 2.5-6% depending on agency. Audax built an AI risk-scoring tool (ToltIQ) applied across its portfolio, finding only 4-6% heavily exposed. He emphasizes fixed charge coverage ratio (not interest coverage) as the binding covenant metric, with fund averages of 1.6-1.8x versus market stretching toward 1.2-1.3x. He discusses BDC redemption stress earlier in 2026 (public BDC redemptions 9-19%, Audax's evergreen fund only ~1.5%), deal flow down 10-16% industry-wide but up 20% for Audax, and skepticism that enough capital exists to fund the full AI buildout, with weaker credits and some data-center projects likely left unfinanced.
terms: ARR loan -- annual recurring revenue loan, where lending is sized against projected/contracted forward revenue growth rather than trailing realized cash flow
LTM EBITDA -- latest twelve months earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a trailing cash-flow measure
fixed charge coverage ratio -- cash flow less fixed charges (taxes, capex, working capital) divided by fixed obligations, a stricter covenant metric than interest coverage
unitranche -- a single blended loan facility combining senior and subordinated debt into one tranche with one all-in rate
BDC -- business development company, a closed-end investment vehicle that lends to middle-market companies
PIK -- payment-in-kind, interest paid by adding to loan principal rather than in cash

8118e65e-0d1c-49d3-842b-daf277a8e268.recap: The host covers Fed Governor Waller's CNBC appearance reiterating that the FOMC may need a 50bp hike in December, arguing firms are successfully passing 3%+ price increases to resilient consumers and that inflation expectations need a 'shock.' Unlike the prior CPI-driven selloff, markets largely ignored him this time: the 10yr sits near 4.05-4.06%, the 2yr near 4.78%, and the curve is flattening in both directions, consistent with weak growth expectations rather than inflation fear. TIPS breakevens, especially longer-dated and 5y5y forward measures, keep pricing very limited risk of sustained, broadening inflation. A key technical point: swap spreads showed no coincident move even as front-end treasury yields were volatile, which the host reads as proof the market is pricing a purely short-run 'Fed risk' rather than any genuine repricing of inflation or growth — a historical parallel is drawn to 2008, when Fed officials similarly dismissed TIPS signals based on anecdotal pass-through evidence and later had to reverse hikes quickly. Separately, the episode flags intensifying credit-market pushback on AI financing: banks are increasingly stuck with 'hung deals' as bridge financing for data-center and M&A deals proves hard to syndicate into HY/loan markets, discouraging further bridge lending. This compounds a broad commodity meltdown (copper, silver, aluminum) despite tight physical supply, read as a demand-side repricing of the AI capex/reflation narrative and China weakness, alongside dollar strength attributed to tightening global funding conditions. A chunk of the episode is an unrelated political/conference pitch, not relevant here.
terms: TIPS -- Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, used to derive market breakeven inflation expectations
breakeven inflation -- the inflation rate implied by the yield gap between nominal Treasuries and TIPS of the same maturity
swap spread -- the difference between a fixed swap rate and the yield on a Treasury of similar maturity, used as a funding/credit risk gauge
hung deal -- a loan or bond deal that a bank has underwritten/bridge-financed but cannot fully syndicate or sell down to investors at the expected terms
bridge financing -- short-term bank lending provided to fund a deal until permanent financing (e.g. bond or syndicated loan issuance) can be arranged
5y5y forward (breakeven) -- the market-implied average inflation rate expected over the five-year period beginning five years from now

omfif.podbean.com/ff9cfe8a-7c4d-38a6-bf7.recap: Mark Sobel interviews FT Alphaville editor Robin Wigglesworth about his book 'A Fabulous Debt,' a history of the bond market. Wigglesworth argues bonds, not stocks, are the economy's true engine, illustrating this through Venice's 1171 war bond (the Prestiti) and Jay Cooke, the Civil War financier whose railway-bond overreach triggered the Panic of 1873. He draws a direct parallel to today's AI boom: like 19th-century railways, AI was initially funded by hyperscalers' free cash flow, but in 2026 financing has shifted toward debt (roughly $500-600bn this year) and increasingly toward creative, suboptimal off-balance-sheet structures reminiscent of the railway era's trust and mortgage bonds — a shift that makes him more uneasy. On regulation, he says the knowledge gap that caused 2008 has narrowed, but he's alarmed by what he calls deliberate political weakening of the SEC, CFTC and Fed supervisory staff (citing a 30% cut to the Fed Board's supervisory/regulatory staff), which he sees as emboldening mainstream Wall Street risk-taking. On sovereign debt, he says default is unthinkable for major economies; the realistic toolkit is a mix of growth, tax increases, spending cuts, financial repression and inflation. He flags France (52 years without a budget surplus, polarized politics) as most worrying, expects the ECB to backstop it regardless, and discusses 'Ferguson's law' (debt service exceeding defense spending signals imperial decline) as a flawed but evocative lens, noting the US breached it in 2024 but faces no real bond-market check given persistent foreign demand for Treasuries.
